events.content: Lagrange's Réflexions on the algebraic solution of equations
events.description: In his 'Réflexions sur la résolution algébrique des équations' (1770–1771), Lagrange examined why the known formulas for the cubic and quartic work, showing that the existing solution methods all depend on the behavior of resolvent expressions when the roots of the equation are permuted. His analysis suggested that these methods could not extend to the quintic, and his study of permutations of the roots laid the groundwork for the theory of permutation groups.

events.content: Ruffini claims a proof that the quintic is unsolvable
events.description: In his two-volume 'Teoria generale delle equazioni' (1799), Ruffini gave the first claimed proof that the general equation of degree five cannot be solved by radicals. Building on Lagrange's ideas about permutations of the roots, his argument contained important early group-theoretic results, but it had a gap and was largely ignored by his contemporaries (Cauchy was a notable exception).

events.content: Abel proves the insolvability of the quintic
events.description: Abel published, at his own expense, a six-page pamphlet ('Mémoire sur les équations algébriques') containing the first complete proof that the general equation of degree five cannot be solved by radicals — the result now known as the Abel–Ruffini theorem. An expanded version appeared in the first volume of Crelle's Journal in 1826.

In his 'Mémoire sur les conditions de résolubilité des équations par radicaux', submitted to the Paris Academy in January 1831, Galois introduced the term 'group' and studied groups of permutations of the roots of an equation as objects in their own right for the first time. He characterized exactly which equations are solvable by radicals in terms of the structure of the associated group, introducing along the way the ideas of normal subgroups and solvability. The Academy rejected the memoir as insufficiently developed, and it remained unpublished at his death in 1832.

events.content: Cauchy develops the theory of permutations
events.description: Beginning with his 1844 'Mémoire sur les arrangements que l'on peut former avec des lettres données', Cauchy published an extensive series of papers developing the fundamentals of permutation theory as a subject of its own: cycle notation and the decomposition of a permutation into cycles, the order of an element, conjugate (similar) permutations, and transpositions. In 1845 he proved that any group of permutations whose order is divisible by a prime p contains an element of order p — Cauchy's theorem.

Fourteen years after Galois's death, Liouville published Galois's principal memoirs in his Journal de mathématiques pures et appliquées (1846), having announced to the Paris Academy that Galois's solvability criterion was correct. This publication finally brought Galois's ideas to the attention of the mathematical community and launched the development of group theory in the following decades.

events.content: Cayley's papers on abstract group theory
events.description: Between 1849 and 1878 Cayley wrote a series of papers on group theory. In 'On the theory of groups, as depending on the symbolic equation θⁿ = 1' (1854), he was the first to define a group abstractly — as a set with an associative operation satisfying the group axioms, rather than as a set of permutations — and introduced group multiplication tables. Returning to the subject in 1878, he stated the result now called Cayley's theorem: every finite group can be represented as a group of permutations.

In his 1872 'Vergleichende Betrachtungen über neuere geometrische Forschungen', published on joining the faculty at Erlangen, Klein proposed classifying geometries by their groups of symmetries: each geometry is the study of the properties left invariant by a given transformation group. The Erlangen Program unified Euclidean, projective, and non-Euclidean geometry under the framework of group theory and made groups central to geometry.

events.content: Dedekind factors the group determinant (unpublished work)
events.description: The group determinant of a finite group G is the determinant of the |G| × |G| matrix whose (g, h) entry is the variable x_{gh⁻¹}. In unpublished notes from 1880, Dedekind showed that when G is abelian this determinant factors into |G| linear forms, one for each character of G. Around 1886 he computed the group determinants of the symmetric group S₃ and the quaternion group and found that they contain irreducible factors of degree two, each occurring squared. Dedekind connected the problem with his 1885 paper on commutative 'hypercomplex' number systems and speculated that enlarging the coefficients to such a system might restore a factorization into linear factors. He put the problem aside, but it is exactly what he handed to Frobenius a decade later.

events.content: Dedekind writes to Frobenius about the group determinant
events.description: In letters of 19 March and 8 April 1896, Dedekind described his old computations of group determinants to Frobenius, with whom he had been corresponding since 1882. He explained the factorization into linear forms for abelian groups, gave the examples of S₃ and the quaternion group where irreducible factors of higher degree appear, and asked what the general rule might be. Frobenius took up the problem immediately.

events.content: Frobenius discovers group characters in letters to Dedekind
events.description: In a rapid series of letters to Dedekind beginning on 12 April 1896, Frobenius worked out the theory of characters for an arbitrary finite group. He defined them not from representations, which came later, but from the multiplication of conjugacy-class sums in the group algebra, and he found the orthogonality relations they satisfy. By the letter of 26 April he had computed the character tables of A₄, A₅, S₄, S₅, and the simple group of order 168, and had seen that the irreducible factors of the group determinant correspond exactly to the characters.

Presented to the Berlin Academy on 16 July 1896, this paper is the birth of the character theory of nonabelian finite groups. Frobenius defined the characters of a finite group by way of the structure constants of the conjugacy classes, proved that the number of characters equals the number of conjugacy classes, and established the two orthogonality relations. The characters here are still not traces of matrices — that interpretation came the following year — but the numerical theory, including the character tables of several small groups, is already complete.

Presented to the Berlin Academy in December 1896, this paper solved Dedekind's problem. Frobenius proved that the group determinant of a finite group G factors as a product of distinct irreducible polynomials Φ₁^f₁ · Φ₂^f₂ ⋯ Φₖ^fₖ, where k is the number of conjugacy classes of G, each Φᵢ is homogeneous of degree fᵢ and corresponds to one of the characters of G, and — the remarkable part — each irreducible factor appears with multiplicity equal to its own degree. It follows that the sum of the squares of the degrees of the characters is |G|. Frobenius's later terminology 'Grad' (degree) of a character comes from this theorem.

events.content: Frobenius defines representations of finite groups by matrices
events.description: In 'Über die Darstellung der endlichen Gruppen durch lineare Substitutionen' (Berlin Sitzungsberichte, 1897), Frobenius introduced the concept of a representation (Darstellung) of a finite group: a homomorphism from the group to a group of invertible matrices. He showed that the characters he had defined the year before are exactly the traces of the irreducible representations, that the irreducible representations correspond to the prime factors of the group determinant, and that every representation can be built from irreducible ones — the last point in a form completed by Maschke in 1899. From this paper on, characters and representations are two sides of a single theory.

Jordan's 'Traité des substitutions et des équations algébriques' (Paris, 1870) was the first book devoted to group theory. It systematized Galois's ideas, developed the theory of permutation groups, and introduced linear groups over finite fields together with the notion of a composition series. Klein and Lie read it during their stay in Paris that spring and summer, and it convinced both of them that groups could organize geometry, not just the theory of equations.

events.content: Lie and Klein together in Paris
events.description: Klein and Lie, who had met in Berlin in the winter of 1869–70, both came to Paris in the spring of 1870 and lived in neighboring rooms in the Latin Quarter. They talked daily, attended Jordan's lectures, studied his newly published Traité, and met Darboux, who taught them the French approach to differential geometry. Lie found his line-to-sphere transformation there and Klein saw the first outlines of what became the Erlangen Program. The Franco-Prussian War broke out on 19 July; Klein, a Prussian, left at once, while Lie set out on foot for Italy and was arrested at Fontainebleau as a spy, his notes mistaken for coded messages, until Darboux secured his release.

In 'Die Grundgleichungen für die elektromagnetischen Vorgänge in bewegten Körpern', presented to the Göttingen Academy on 21 December 1907 and preceded by a 5 November lecture to the Göttingen Mathematical Society on 'Das Relativitätsprinzip', Minkowski rewrote Lorentz's and Einstein's relativity as geometry. He introduced the four-dimensional space-time with coordinates x, y, z, it, showed that the Lorentz transformations are exactly the linear maps preserving x² + y² + z² − c²t², and named this group G_c, the Lorentz group. The principle of relativity became the statement that the laws of physics are the invariants of this group, in the spirit of the Erlangen Program.

In his lecture 'Raum und Zeit' at the Assembly of German Natural Scientists and Physicians in Cologne on 21 September 1908, Minkowski presented the geometric view of relativity to a general scientific audience. He contrasted the Galilean group G_∞ of Newtonian mechanics with the Lorentz group G_c, introduced the light cone, world lines, and proper time, and declared that space and time by themselves would fade into shadows, leaving only a union of the two. The lecture, published in 1909 shortly after his death, fixed the picture of special relativity as the geometry of Minkowski space-time under the Lorentz group.
